knownFor: Bishop of Alexandria who defended the faith of Nicaea through five exiles and wrote against Arius and his heirs.

traces: The church historian Socrates of Constantinople declines to tell Antony's story because Athanasius of Alexandria had already given a whole book to it. Evagrius, later bishop at Antioch, put that book into Latin with a short apology for how freely he rendered it.
Gregory of Nazianzus gave him a whole sermon at Constantinople, and in it says that all who have lived according to God still live to God.

In 433 Cyril of Alexandria wrote to John of Antioch that some had garbled Athanasius of Alexandria's letter to Epictetus of Corinth. He sent transcripts from old copies he held, which he called genuine.
remembered: Honored sixty years after his death: Cyril of Alexandria singles him out among the Fathers whose teaching he refuses to step outside of.
Disputed in his own time: the bishops at Tyre deposed him, and the reasons for his exile to Trier were reported two ways, as Socrates of Constantinople's telling shows.

uncertain: How Arsenius reached Tyre is not settled. Socrates of Constantinople credits God's providence: the governor's servants heard at an inn that he was hiding in a citizen's house, and the governor had him found. The church historian Sozomen gives two reasons, a divine prompting or, "as it is said", a plan of Athanasius of Alexandria. He says Arsenius slipped into Tyre by night the day before the trial.

The historian Rufinus of Aquileia tells that Bishop Alexander of Alexandria once watched boys on the shore playing at church, and that the boy who played bishop was young Athanasius of Alexandria. Socrates of Constantinople, who names Rufinus as his source, thinks it not improbable, and Sozomen tells it too.
Socrates of Constantinople says Athanasius of Alexandria hid for four months in a family tomb. The Historia Acephala, a record of his life, says he went to a country house of his near the New River.

briefReferences: Festal Index VIII, ed. Archibald Robertson: the council at Tyre in 335, dated by its consuls.
Socrates, Church History I.27, tr. A. C. Zenos: the churches divided over Arius; the charge of the severed hand, Arsenius and magic.
Socrates, Church History I.29, tr. Zenos: Arsenius found, led in with his hands under his cloak, and both hands shown. Socrates writes with plain sympathy for Athanasius.
Sozomen, Church History II.25, tr. Chester D. Hartranft: the rumor that Athanasius had hidden Arsenius; the council's deposition of him.
Socrates, Church History I.8, tr. Zenos: Athanasius a deacon at Nicaea, speaking strongly against the Arian party.
Athanasius, Discourse against the Arians I.5, ed. Robertson: extracts from Arius's Thalia, that God was not always a Father and the Son was made out of nothing.
Athanasius, On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea, Eusebius's letter, ed. Robertson: the creed of Nicaea, "begotten not made".
Athanasius, Discourse against the Arians II, ed. Robertson: if the Son were a creature, man's becoming man would leave humanity as it was, not joined to God.
Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54, ed. Robertson: "For He was made man that we might be made God".
Socrates, Church History I.35, tr. Zenos: Constantine sends him to Trier over the grain ships, though some said it was for the unity of the church, since he would not hold communion with Arius.
Festal Index, ed. Robertson: the entries for the four later flights; his return to his church a few days after his last withdrawal, which the edition dates to February 366; and his death in 373.

Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21.35, tr. Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow: the dispute over hypostases and persons; Athanasius found they meant the same, let each keep its words, and bound them together in unity of action.

Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21.33, tr. Browne and Swallow: Athanasius's written confession of the unity of Godhead in Father, Son and Spirit, presented to the emperor, and Gregory's claim that few dared to write it.
Athanasius, Life of Antony, preface, ed. Robertson: his account of the hermit's story.
Jerome, Letter 127.5, tr. W. H. Fremantle: Marcella of Rome hearing of Antony's life from Athanasius and taking up that life.
Cyril of Alexandria, Letter to John of Antioch, ed. P. E. Pusey: "our blessed and all-celebrated Father Athanasius". The year 433 is the edition's date.
World census, Alexandrian Catechetical / Christian-Platonist Tradition: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: He became human so that we might be made God.
quotationOriginals.printed: He was made man that we might be made God.
quotationOriginals.work: Athanasius, On the Incarnation 54, ed. Robertson
quotationOriginals.uncertain: "We might be made God" keeps the passive of the Greek: God does the deifying. "We might become God" is a second reading that loses this.

quotationOriginals.modern: our blessed Father Athanasius, praised by all.
quotationOriginals.printed: our blessed and all-celebrated Father Athanasius.
quotationOriginals.work: Cyril of Alexandria, Letter to John of Antioch, ed. P. E. Pusey
quotationOriginals.uncertain: "All-celebrated" means praised by everyone. "Highly honored" is a weaker second reading.
